System design should clearly define what the system is expected to do. This includes linking functional and non-functional requirements to the intended end user of each requirement, as well as explaining why that user needs the specified functionality. Adjustments to system functions and capabilities should be made based on budget constraints and the preferences and needs of end users. Digital tracking and decision support (DTDS) systems, the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11), the Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine (SNOMED), and universal health coverage (UHC) are key components in this context. Overview of Components: 1. Health Interventions and Recommendations: No specific notations are used. 2. Generic Personas: No specific notations are used. 3. User Scenarios: No specific notations are used. 4. Business Processes and Workflows: Each workflow should have a process name and a corresponding identifier (e.g., A, B7, CHE.1). Digital adaptation kits (DAKs) and identification (ID) are integral to this process. Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) for Child Health in Emergencies: The DAK is designed for health program managers within ministries of health (MOH) who collaborate with digital health and health information systems counterparts to determine health content requirements for child health in humanitarian emergencies. These managers oversee and monitor the implementation of clinical practices and policies in this area. The DAK also supports individuals responsible for translating health system processes and guidance documents into digital systems, providing essential components to initiate the development of a DTDS system in a standards-compliant manner. These individuals, often referred to as business analysts, act as intermediaries between health content experts and software development teams. The DAK includes critical outputs such as data dictionaries and decision-support algorithms to ensure the validity and consistency of health content within the DTDS system. Collaboration between health program managers and digital health counterparts is essential for using the DAK effectively. Although each DAK focuses on a specific health program area (e.g., child health in emergencies), they are designed to be modular and link to other health program areas within primary healthcare settings, promoting integration across services. Scenarios for Using the DAK: 1. Incorporating WHO Guidelines into Existing DTDS Systems: Countries with existing digital systems, such as electronic medical records and decision-support tools, can use the DAK to verify alignment with WHO guidelines. Users can extract specific decision algorithms for integration into their systems and identify differences in workflows, data inputs, and decision-support logic to understand local adaptations of guideline content. 2. Transitioning from Paper to DTDS Systems: Countries with paper-based systems can use the DAK as a starting point to streamline data elements and decision-support requirements for optimized digital systems. Reviewing paper-based tools can help identify missing fields or content for inclusion in the digital system. WHO recommendations, such as those for optimizing health worker roles, provide stepwise guidance for mapping paper-based data into digital systems. 3. Linking Aggregate Reporting Systems to Point-of-Care DTDS Systems: Some countries may have digital systems for aggregate reporting but lack service delivery-level digital systems. The DAK provides aggregate indicators derived from individual-level data to bridge these levels. Indicators and performance metrics should be consulted to support routine data use at facility and district levels. 4. Leveraging Data Standards for Interoperability and Integration: The DAK includes data elements mapped to ICD codes and other standards to support the design of interoperable systems. The data dictionary provides necessary codes for different data elements, reducing implementation time for global standards in digital system design. Broader Digital Health Ecosystem: DAKs are part of the broader digital health ecosystem and should be used within a strategic vision by the MOH for implementing DTDS systems. In contexts lacking such a vision, users should consult resources like the WHO-ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, WHO recommendations on digital interventions, and the WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide to select and apply appropriate digital health interventions. Guidelines for the Management of Common Childhood Illnesses: The Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children is a resource for doctors, nurses, and health workers responsible for the care of young children in first-level referral hospitals. It is based on evidence from WHO clinical guidelines and is intended for use in both inpatient and outpatient care in small hospitals with basic laboratory facilities and essential medicines. The guidelines focus on managing major causes of childhood mortality in developing countries, such as newborn problems, pneumonia, diarrhea, malaria, meningitis, sepsis, measles, severe acute malnutrition, and pediatric HIV/AIDS. They also cover some common surgical conditions manageable in small hospitals. Advanced treatment options like intensive care or mechanical ventilation are not included. These guidelines are adaptable to country-specific circumstances and aim to support the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI).
